[1]

Plaintiff
is an active member of the Department of Anesthesia at the McGill University
Health Center (“MUHC”) since over ten years as a result of privileges granted
to him by the MUHC board of directors. He practices at the Royal Victoria
Hospital (“RVH”) site of the Glen campus.

[2]

The relations between the physicians in the RVH
Anesthesia Department are fraught with conflict. A law suit has been instituted
in 2017 by certain members against the majority group.

[3]

In October 2019, there is a heated confrontation
between Plaintiff and the RVH Department of Anesthesia site director. As a
result, the site director filed a complaint against Plaintiff for what he
considered to be unacceptable behaviour. Plaintiff then took a leave of
absence.

[4]

Pursuant to the site director’s complaint, an
investigation was carried out by a medical examiner as is called for in such
matters by the
Act respecting health services and social services
(“
AHSS
”).
[1]
The medical examiner
eventually concluded that it was not necessary to transfer the matter for
disciplinary action to the MUHC’s Council of Physicians, Dentists and
Pharmacists. A review of the medical examiners’ decision asked for by the site
director was also dismissed by a Review Committee.

[5]

In February 2020, Plaintiff asked to return to
the RVH from his leave. However, his treating physician asked that his return
be carried out on a progressive basis and set out various accommodations that
were required.

[6]

After some back and forth on his condition, the
MUHC decided to relegate him to a private clinic with whom the MUHC had
undertaken, by agreement, to provide an anesthesiologist
[2]
to catch up on the surgery
back log created by the COVID-19 pandemic. The work he carries out at the
private clinic for surgeries related to the MUHC accounts for two and half to
three days. Plaintiff also works in surgeries which do not originate from the
MUHC. Since the summer of 2020, he works four days per week at the private
clinic.

[7]

The MUHC is therefore of the opinion that they
are allowing him to exercise his privileges.

[8]

Plaintiff replies that being relegated to a
private clinic is in fact a limitation and modification of his privileges and a
sanction which was carried out without following the legal requirements or due
process. The procedures he carries out at the private clinic are not comparable
in complexity to those which he carried out at the MUHC and do not allow him to
practice his subspecialty. He does not teach and cannot work on his research
projects.

[9]

Plaintiff claims that the MUHC is violating his
rights under the
Quebec
Charter of human rights and freedoms
[3]
by acting in a discriminatory
manner. The MUHC should provide him with reasonable accommodations given his
condition and allow him to carry out a progressive reintegration at the RVH
site, the whole in accordance with his physician’s recommendations.

[10]

The MUHC responds that Plaintiff has not been able to carry out his
full privileges since late 2017. By continuing to insist on further
accommodations, he is imposing undue hardship on the institution. These
accommodations have deleterious effects on other staff members of the
Department of Anesthesia and negatively impact quality of care and patient
safety. They also raise the facts that Plaintiff has been the subject of
complaints of residents.

[11]

The Court now has to determine whether it will order the MUHC, by
way of interlocutory injunction, to allow Plaintiff to return to practice at
the RVH site, as per his physician’s reintegration plan.
[4]

[12]

No provisional nor safeguard orders have been rendered.

[13]

The record on which the Court has to base its decision to decide the
application for interlocutory relief is constituted of nine (9) detailed
affidavits, transcripts of the cross examination of seven of the affiants,
Plaintiff’s 51 exhibits and Defendant’s 50 exhibits. No witnesses were heard
viva
voce
before the Court.

[
14
]

The matter is not yet set down for trial.

[
15
]

There are therefore three issues in litigation:

1. Does Plaintiff have a serious right?

2. Is he suffering irreparable harm?

3. Does the
balance of inconveniences favour issuing interlocutory relief?

[
16
]

Prior to discussing these issues, the Court must first deal with a
request for anonymity, non-publication and confidentiality sought by Plaintiff.

ANONYMITY
AND CONFIDENTIALITY

[
17
]

Plaintiff alleges that his application, the affidavits in support
thereof and several of the exhibits in its support contain “private, sensitive
and detailed information” about his “personal health situation, in particular
with respect to a recently-diagnosed medical condition”.
[5]
If this information were to
become public, it would cause him “serious and irreparable reputational harm,
in particular with his colleagues and students at the MUHC and within the
circle of anesthesiologists in Québec and beyond”.
[6]

[
18
]

Plaintiff claims that but for MUHC’s refusal, he would not have to
bring these proceedings, and thereby risk that private, sensitive and detailed
information about his personal situation be made public and thus further
serious reputational harm be caused.

[
19
]

Plaintiff therefore asks this Court to order the following measures:

(a) An order barring the MUHC from
communicating information with respect to the present proceedings or Dr. Waters
to any person other than the undersigned attorneys and the MUHC’s legal
counsel, unless otherwise ordered by this Court;

(b) An order to redact certain
sections of the present proceedings from the public record and to keep certain
exhibits under seal;

(c) An order to anonymize Dr.
Waters’ identity and to authorize the use of initials for the public record in
the present proceedings;

(d) A non-publication order.

[
20
]

The honourable Bachand, then at the Superior Court, issued certain
orders at the outset of the file, for a limited ten day period.
[7]
The honourable Suzanne
Courchesne then rendered an order of confidentiality and anonymity to remain in
place until an interlocutory judgment was rendered.
[8]
In particular, she ordered
that certain sections of the application and of Plaintiff’s affidavit be
redacted from the public record, that his identity be kept confidential by all
means and that his initials be used and that no element related to the present
file be published until an interlocutory judgment was rendered.

[
21
]

These orders were not contested at the time by the MUHC.

[
22
]

At the interlocutory injunction hearing before the Court, the MUHC
deferred to the Court’s discretion in such matters.

[
23
]

The Court is now in a position to fully appreciate the issues
relating to confidentiality having reviewed in great detail all the exhibits
both in demand and in defense. The MUHC has made its position known through
several affidavits. Plaintiff filed an affidavit of a third party. Lengthy
cross-examinations occurred of all affiants.

[
24
]

In order to decide this issue of confidentiality and anonymity, the
Court must follow the reasons set out by the Court of appeal in
Lamontagne
.
[9]
They are most aptly summarized
by the honorable Sheehan in
Dis son nom
in the following twelve succinct
propositions:
[10]

14.1.    L’article 11 du Code de
procédure civile confirme le caractère public de la procédure devant les
tribunaux judiciaires. Ce principe est intimement lié à la liberté d’expression
et à la liberté de presse qui sont toutes deux garanties par l’
alinéa 2b)
de la

Charte canadienne des droits et libertés
. Ces droits fondamentaux assurent au
public l’accès à l’information provenant des activités des différentes cours de
justice au pays.

14.2.    Le caractère public des
débats judiciaires constitue une composante essentielle de la démocratie
canadienne. Le respect de ce principe maintient le niveau de transparence
requis pour l’examen critique des tribunaux et de leur fonctionnement. Cette
transparence favorise « la confiance du public dans la probité du système
judiciaire et la compréhension de l’administration de la justice ».

14.3.    Une justice publique
participe à la promotion et à la reconnaissance de ces valeurs
constitutionnelles que sont l’indépendance et l’impartialité des tribunaux, des
composantes fondamentales qui permettent d’assurer la légitimité du processus
judiciaire.

14.4.    L’identité des
intervenants au processus judiciaire constitue l’un des aspects de la publicité
des débats. Une personne qui recherche le secours des tribunaux doit en
principe le faire ouvertement en accord avec la transparence dont doit faire
preuve le système de justice. Le fait d’ester en justice comporte donc le
risque implicite pour le justiciable d’être contraint de dévoiler des questions
de nature strictement personnelle.

14.5.    La possibilité d’une
atteinte à la réputation, la honte et l’embarras ne sont généralement pas
suffisants pour justifier une demande d’anonymat. Le principe de la publicité
des débats devant normalement primer, le secret demeure l’exception.

14.6.    Néanmoins, la
jurisprudence tempère la portée du principe général de la publicité des débats
dans les cas où « la protection des valeurs sociales doit prévaloir sur la
transparence des procédures judiciaires ».

14.7.    Ainsi, les tribunaux ont
permis de procéder de façon anonyme en matière de cyberintimidation à caractère
sexuel envers une mineure, dans les cas d’aide médicale à mourir, dans une action
collective réclamant le remboursement des frais d’avortement, dans un cas où le
demandeur avait subi des menaces de mort ou encore lorsque la déconsidération
des proches était susceptible de causer un tort évitable à une partie.

14.8.    Le législateur accorde
aussi d’emblée l’anonymat aux parties impliquées dans certains litiges,
notamment en matières familiales (articles 15 et 16 du Code de procédure
civile).

14.9.    Ces dérogations reposent
pour l’essentiel sur l’application judicieuse de la notion de la bonne
administration de la justice. Le principe de la publicité des débats
judiciaires doit donc être modulé lorsque nécessaire pour préserver la capacité
du justiciable à recourir aux tribunaux pour exercer ses droits, incluant ses
droits fondamentaux. Il faut éviter que l’application sans nuance du principe
de la publicité des débats puisse constituer un frein à l’accès à la justice.

[References provided in the
original text are omitted].

[
25
]

The Court of Appel in
Lamontagne
sets out the two pronged
test developed by the Supreme Court in
Dagenais
[11]
and
Mentuck,
[12]
and summarized in
Globe
and Mail
:

1.

Are the measures sought necessary to protect an important legal
interest and impair free expression as little as possible? If alternative
measures can just as effectively protect the interests engaged, the restriction
is unjustified;

2.

If no such alternatives exist, the inquiry turns to whether the
proper balance was struck between the open court principle and the privacy
rights.

[
26
]

To decide on Plaintiff’s request, the Court finds the following
facts to be relevant, which will be more extensively discussed in the reasons
dealing with the criteria which apply to the application for interlocutory
injunctive relief:

26.1.

The MUHC Department of the Anesthesia at the RVH
is strife torn since many years. Proceedings have been instituted, amongst
others by the Plaintiff. These are public.

26.2.

Plaintiff took a leave of absence in December
2017 due to an undisclosed medical condition. His leave was obvious for all to
see in the Department.

26.3.

When he progressively reintegrated his position
in early 2018, accommodations were asked by his treating physician and granted
by the MUHC. They included lightening of loads for cardiac surgery and for
procedures requiring wearing of lead gowns and no on-call duty. Most likely,
this difference in treatment were for all to see in the Department.

26.4.

In the fall of 2019, a heated altercation
occurred between Plaintiff and the site director which seems to be the
proximate cause of the dispute which brings the parties before the Court today.
This was carried out in a public space, even though it is not clear if the
witnesses heard what had been exchanged.

26.5.

Plaintiff then took a five month leave, before
declaring himself available to be progressively reintegrated in March 2020. It
was obvious to all in the department that Plaintiff was on leave.

26.6.

Residents have been consulted in a survey and
have made their discomfort known in no uncertain terms regarding the hostility
amongst two groups of anesthesiologists at the RVH site. Plaintiff is
explicitly identified as being part of one group.

26.7.

His physician sets out a detailed plan of
progressive reintegration over a period of months: first one day, then two and
moving to four. At the end of this period, still no call duty and a lighter
cardiac surgery load. Furthermore, accommodations are required regarding
respiratory technicians. Again, the Court can but conclude that these
accommodations would be for all to see as they would be evident on the
scheduling and would have impact on other members of staff.

26.8.

It is at this point that the MUHC insisted that
it obtain a better understanding of his medical condition before agreeing to
his return. Plaintiff provided a one page letter of a specialist providing
little other information on his condition than identifying the diagnosis.
Meetings were held with specialists.

26.9.

Despite the reams of evidence filed by both
parties, the Court has no understanding of the medical history of the
Plaintiff’s condition, its symptoms nor its treatment.

26.10.

The Plaintiff has been practicing up to four
days a week at Rockland MD since the summer of 2020 and there is no debate that
his medical condition does not impede him from so doing.

26.11.

There is in fact no true debate as to whether
his medical condition
per se
prevents him from carrying out his
privileges. What is the subject of debate however, is to what extent the
specific accommodations sought by the Plaintiff’s specialist, must be agreed to
by the MUHC and if they constitute undue hardship.

26.12.

It is Plaintiff which is seeking these
accommodations. If they were to be put in effect, they would be plain for all
to see and would have impacts on others, as regards scheduling, allocation of
resources, cardiac surgery load and on call duty.

26.13.

It is the level of impact and inconvenience this
may cause to staff and patients which is the crux of the matter, not to
assessing whether the underlying condition prevents the Plaintiff from carrying
out his full duties.

26.14.

In this regard, it must be assessed by the
Court whether a four weekday case load at a private clinic is an appropriate
solution, given the level of accommodation sought. Once again, the fact that
Plaintiff works full time at the private clinic and not at the RVH site is
plain for all to see.

[
27
]

Given the above, the Court concludes that the dispute between the
Plaintiff and the partnership is a public legal matter. The 2019 dispute was
held in a public space.

[
28
]

His 2017 leave of absence and the gist of the accommodations that
were extended to him upon his return were known by any person working in the
Department. His leave in 2019 was necessarily observed by all who would have
dealt with him at the MUHC.

[
29
]

The fact that he now works four days at a private clinic is also
inescapable for any observer. If he was to return progressively, following the
accommodations which he requests, this would also be of public knowledge.

[
30
]

The Plaintiff has therefore not convinced the Court that the
concerns he raises are sufficient to justify his anonymity and the
non-publication of the file.

[
31
]

Plaintiff wants to force the MUHC to run its department taking into
account an eventual Court order. He is not simply asking the MUHC to abstain or
cease and desist to do something. The order he seeks will have implications for
several individuals. These implications would even extend beyond the MUHC and
its employees. Physicians working at the RVH site are not employees. They hold
privileges to work at the MUHC. The order will also affect the organization of
care at the private clinic and at the McGill University Faculty of Medicine and
will potentially impact government officials.

[
32
]

Plaintiff’s request is simply unrealistic and untenable. If the MUHC
must put into effect a judgment, clearly against the will of several
individuals, while maintaining the anonymity of the Plaintiff or, worse,
respecting a non-publication ban of the judgment which explains why it is
acting in a manner which could be seen as heavy handed, there will just be more
conflict.

[
33
]

The Supreme Court in
Canadian Broadcasting Corp.

underlines that
justice done openly has become “one of the hallmarks of a democratic society”.
The Supreme Court stresses that ‘the open court principle, seen as “the very
soul of justice” and the “security of securities”, acts as a guarantee that
justice is administered in a non-arbitrary manner, according to the rule of law”.
Hence, “openness was held to be the rule, covertness the exception, thereby
fostering public confidence in the integrity of the court system and
understanding of the administration of justice”.
[13]

[
34
]

The Court hopes that this judgment will serve to contribute to bring
a certain measure of peace and harmony in the RVH Department of Anesthesia for
the sake of plaintiff, defendants, all the staff that works at the MUHC and,
most importantly, patients. In this regard, the Court deems it essential that
the decision which it renders and the reasons that it provides will indeed
foster public confidence in the process that was followed and ensure an
understanding of the Court’s reasons.

[
35
]

That being said, there is no need that any details of Plaintiff’s
health or condition be made public or discussed in this judgment. The parties
have not made his medical condition a subject of debate.

[
36
]

What is a subject of debate is the level of accommodation he seeks.
Hence, the Court will order that exhibits P-12 and P-12A are kept confidential
and that they be held in the court record under seal. It will also keep the
Originating Application for the Issuance of Interlocutory and Permanent
Injunctions and the Amended version of March 12, 2021 under seal, and will ask
Plaintiff to file a redacted version of the Amended Originating Application in
the Court record within ten days of the judgment to be rendered, blacking out
s. 80.40.2 thereof.

[
37
]

Given that Plaintiff contends that the lack of anonymity and the
publication of the judgment could cause him significant and irreparable harm,
the Court will lift the Order of confidentiality ordered by Justice Courchesne
effective as of May 24, 2021. This will allow Plaintiff to take measures if he
believes the Court’s refusal to so order warrants review.

ANALYSIS

[
38
]

In order to succeed on his demand for interlocutory injunctive
relief, plaintiff must convince the Court that there is a serious issue to be
tried,
[14]

that the person applying for the injunction will suffer irreparable harm if the
injunction were not granted and that the balance of convenience favours
granting the interlocutory injunction.

1.

S
erious issue to be
tried

[
39
]

The Court of Appeal sets out in
CRH
that the right which
Plaintiff invokes must stand out as a result of a preliminary analysis of the
file: “Ce critère est généralement peu exigeant. Il
suffit que la demande ne soit ni frivole ni vexatoire. Par conséquent, un long
examen du bien-fondé de la demande n'est souvent ni nécessaire ni souhaitable”.
[15]

[
40
]

Unfortunately, the multi-faceted and long history of the dispute
forces the Court to undergo a “long examen du bien fondé”. However, at the end
of this process, the serious issue to be tried criteria is not demanding and
the Court is of the opinion that Plaintiff meets it.

1.1.3

Duty to accommodate

[
86
]

Art. 10
of the
Quebec Charter
stipulates that “every person
has a right to full and equal recognition and exercise of his human rights and
freedoms, without distinction, exclusion or preference based on (…) a handicap or
the use of any means to palliate a handicap”. “Discrimination exists where such
a distinction, exclusion or preference has the effect of nullifying or
impairing such right”.

[
87
]

The
Quebec Charter
contains specific provisions dealing with
discrimination in the context of employment:

16. No one may practise
discrimination in respect of the hiring, apprenticeship, duration of the
probationary period, vocational training, promotion, transfer, displacement,
laying-off, suspension, dismissal or conditions of employment of a person or in
the establishment of categories or classes of employment.

[
88
]

The Supreme Court in
McGill University Health Center
explains
that discrimination occurs when arbitrary barriers are imposed which are based
on attributed abilities, and not actual ones.
[67]

[
89
]

The duty not to discriminate carries with it a corollary duty to
accommodate a “disabled employee”. The Supreme Court in
Caron
, sets out
the basis of this “fundamental tenet of Quebec labour law”:
[68]

[22] The
duty to reasonably accommodate disabled employees is a fundamental tenet of
Canadian and, more particularly, Quebec labour law. The goal of the duty to accommodate
in the employment context was summarized by Deschamps J. as being “to ensure
that an employee who is able to work can do so....
The purpose of the duty
to accommodate is to ensure that persons who are otherwise fit to work are not
unfairly excluded where working conditions can be adjusted without undue
hardship
[…]. The duty reflects a choice by legislatures to ensure “that
the standards governing the performance of work should be designed to reflect
all members of society, in so far as this is reasonably possible” [Citations
omitted].

[The
Court’s underlinings; citations omitted]

[
90
]

Chief Justice Beverly MacLachlin, as she then was, explains in
Grismer

that “incorporating accommodation into the standard itself ensures that
each person is assessed according to her or his own personal abilities, instead
of being judged against presumed group characteristics”.
[69]

[
91
]

Madame Justice L’Heureux-Dubé stresses in
Montreal (City)

that “with respect to employment, its more specific objective is to eliminate
exclusion that is arbitrary and based on preconceived ideas concerning personal
characteristics which, when the duty to accommodate is taken into account, do
not affect a person’s ability to do a job”.
[70]

[
92
]

As the Supreme Court explains in
Caron
,
the duty to
accommodate an employee is not unlimited: “its scope in any particular case is
defined by the symmetrical concepts of “reasonable accommodation” and “undue
hardship”.
[71]

[
93
]

Undue hardship does not only arise when it is impossible to
accommodate the employee. Indeed, Madam Justice Deschamps explains in
Hydro-Québec

that “the purpose of the duty to accommodate is not to completely alter the
essence of the contract of employment, that is, the employee’s duty to perform
work in exchange for remuneration”.
[72]

She adds that:

[16] The test is not whether it was
impossible for the employer to accommodate the employee’s characteristics.
The
employer does not have a duty to change working conditions in a fundamental
way, but does have a duty, if it can do so without undue hardship, to arrange
the employee’s workplace or duties to enable the employee to do his or her work
.

[The Court’s underlinings]

[
94
]

Therefore, for there to be undue hardship, it must appear that “the
characteristics of an illness are such that the proper operation of the
business is hampered excessively or if an employee with such an illness remains
unable to work for the reasonably foreseeable future even though the employer
has tried to accommodate him or her”.
[73]

Madam Justice Deschamps concludes:

[19] The duty to accommodate is
therefore perfectly compatible with general labour law rules, including both
the rule that employers must respect employees’ fundamental rights and the rule
that employees must do their work.
The employer’s duty to accommodate ends
where the employee is no longer able to fulfill the basic obligations
associated with the employment relationship for the foreseeable future
.

[The Court’s underlinings]

[
95
]

In
Caron
, Madam Justice Abella further insists on the breadth
of the symmetrical concepts of reasonable accommodation and undue hardship:

[29]      Most recently, Gascon J.
in his reasons in
Stewart
v.
Elk Valley Coal Corp
.,
2017 SCC 30
(CanLII)
, [2017] 1 S.C.R. 591, dissenting but not on this point, summarized the
operative principles: an employer is not required to establish that it is
“impossible to accommodate”, only that nothing else reasonable or practical
could be offered
; an individualized analysis is required; the duty to
accommodate includes both procedural and substantive duties; and the undue
hardship threshold means an employer will always bear some sort of hardship

(paras. 125-28).

[The Court’s underlinings]

[
96
]

In
CHU de Québec – Université Laval
, the Court of Appeal has
stated that the employer’s process “doit être sérieuse” and that the
intervenors must “explorer toutes les avenues possibles”.
[74]

[
97
]

The aforementioned Supreme Court cases are rendered in an employment
setting. A physician who holds privileges is not
per se
an employee.
[75]
Nevertheless, the carrying
out of any powers, duties or obligations by the MUHC, including by the DPS and
the Head of Department, under the
AHSS
, in relation to these privileges,
including the granting or renewal or privileges and the manner in which these
privileges are exercised, must be interpreted in accordance with the
Quebec
Charter
values.

[
98
]

In
Caron
, Madam Justice Abella, after having cited Justice
Lebel’s statements in
Communauté urbaine de Montréal
,
[76]
concludes that his approach
“endorses the view that all Quebec law should be interpreted in conformity with
the
Quebec Charter
”.
[77]

She concludes that the duty to accommodate is a core principle of the
Quebec
Charter.
[78]

[
99
]

The case law developed in employment and labour law dealing with
reasonable accommodation and undue hardship, and the necessary symmetry called
for, is therefore highly relevant in interpreting the mutual obligations of
Plaintiff and the MUHC.

[
100
]

However, the broader mission of the university health centres

them the right to exercise clinical activities in a tertiary or quaternary
university health centre. They also entail teaching duties and research. At all
times while he was holding his privileges at the MUHC, he has worked almost
exclusively at the RVH site.

[
249
]

When Plaintiff took his leave of absence in October 2019, it was
agreed that he would return to exercise his privileges at the RVH site.

[
250
]

The Court concludes that in the abstract, relegating Plaintiff to
work for limited periods at a Private Clinic, where the clinical work is not
comparable to that carried out at the MUHC site and where there is no teaching
and no research work, is a modification to his privileges which can only be
carried out by the Board through the disciplinary mechanisms set out in the
AHSS

given the absence of administrative sanctions in departmental rules and
regulations.

[
251
]

Plaintiff is the only RVH Department of Anesthesia member who is systematically
relegated to the Private Clinic.

[
252
]

The Court is of the view that there is a very strong
prima facie

case that his relegation to a Private Clinic has been taken by the MUHC and in
particular by the DPS and the Head of Department as a sanction of what the MUHC
sees as
conduct
of Plaintiff.

[
253
]

According to the MUHC, this measure is meant to appease conflict in
the department and to resolve alleged mistreatment of residents. It is not
related to the organization of the resources as contemplated in case law.

[
254
]

It is inescapable that the Head of the Anesthesia Department is
attempting to prevent by all means Plaintiff to return to the RVH.

[
255
]

He demonstrates a very high level of hostility towards Plaintiff. He
has repeatedly been part of efforts to attempt to bring the Plaintiff to leave
the RVH since 2013. In 2019, he signs a virulent letter in which he makes
statements about Plaintiff’s mental health and indicates that he is a danger to
patients. He signs this letter even though he has no diagnosis whatsoever of
Plaintiff, does not work principally at the RVH site and has never had any
access to his medical records.

[
256
]

The Head of Department’s efforts to torpedo Plaintiff’s career at
the MUHC are intensified after the October 2019 confrontation between Plaintiff
and Daloze. Indeed:

256.1.

He only obtains Daloze’s version of the facts;

256.2.

He encourages Daloze to file a complaint against
Plaintiff;

256.3.

He attends the October 17, 2019 meeting called
by the DPS and then intensely questions the Plaintiff with regard to his
allegations of Daloze’s improper behaviour; he comes back to a familiar refrain
that “The conflict with the group of five has now escalated to a level that
needs urgent and definite solution”;
[171]

256.4.

In parallel, he marshals all the site directors
to boycott Plaintiff if the DPS were to decide to transfer the Plaintiff to
work at any of these sites; he writes that in an email;

256.5.

When the DPS advises him of Plaintiff’s request
to return from his leave of absence in February 2020 he again writes that
nobody from the RVH leadership will be willing to assign Plaintiff any clinical
duties should his return be forced on them;

256.6.

At the ad hoc medical meeting in July 2020, the
Associate Dean concludes that all the difficulties with the residents stem from
the group of five dissidents. The Court can only draw the conclusion that this
version emanates from the Head of Department; it certainly does not flow from
the survey;

256.7.

In July 2020, it is decided by the MUHC that
Plaintiff will be working strictly at the Private Clinic;

256.8.

In late July, when the Medical Examiner renders
his decision concluding that no disciplinary action is required, the Head of
Department writes a scathing criticism of this report.

[
257
]

The Head of Department’s behaviour throughout this process is
inappropriate. He knows or should know what are the limits of his powers and
his role, as well as those of the DPS, the DPCP and its disciplinary committee,
the Medical Examiner and the Board and which were discussed in detail in
section 1.1 of this judgment. Indeed, throughout, the DPS has reminded him of
the strict criteria that must be met if disciplinary measures are taken.

[
258
]

To put it bluntly, the Anesthesia Department of the MUHC is not his
fiefdom where he has the last word on how physicians can carry out their
privileges and how these can be limited. The
AHSS
is not drafted this
way.

[
259
]

If physicians are not conducting themselves inappropriately, save
for his limited powers to impose administrative sanctions for allocation of
resources which he cannot invoke since there are no departmental rules which
call for them, and save for his power to suspend privileges on an urgent 10
days basis, sanctioning of conduct of any of the department’s physicians must
be dealt with by the Board through the clear mechanisms set out in the
AHSS
.

[
260
]

Indeed, the analysis carried out above in section 1.1 highlights
that the finely crafted mechanisms of the
AHSS
not only ensure that
rational decisions are made with regard to patients’, the institutions’ and the
physicians’ best interest, but that the physicians who could be impacted
negatively are subject to a clear procedure which guarantees due process and procedural
fairness, including resort to the TAQ.

[
261
]

Since the consequences on a physician whose conduct is called into
question can be dire, the procedural fairness guarantees that will be accorded
to him before a decision is taken, save in case of emergency, will be at the
stricter end of the procedural fairness sliding scale. The Board, which is
composed in significant part of independent members, is the cornerstone of this
procedural fairness.

[
262
]

The Head of Department rides roughshod over these procedural fairness
guarantees. He tirelessly wants to exclude Plaintiff from the Department, and
this dates back to 2013.

[
263
]

The October 2019 confrontation was the subject of a complaint which,
as per the requirements of the
AHSS
, was dealt with by the Medical
Examiner. He came to the conclusion that no disciplinary action was required. If
he had been of the opinion that the complaint warranted disciplinary action,
the CDPD would then have set up a committee to carry out a disciplinary
investigation. If this committee had been of the opinion that the Board should
impose disciplinary measures, the executive director of the institution would
notify the physician and the reasons therefor. If the Board decided to take
disciplinary measures, it would notify the physician. Due process would be
granted.

[
264
]

It bears repeating that none of this did occur because the Medical
Examiner concluded that there were no grounds to transfer the matter to the
CDPD.

[
265
]

The Site Director then asked for a review by the Review Committee.
This Committee came to the conclusion that the complaint had been fairly and
diligently examined by the Medical Examiner. It noted that “Dr. Waters has
expressed regret for the conversation he had with you and we trust the
situation will not be repeated”. The Review Committee stressed that its
decision was “final”.

[
266
]

The Court need not discuss whether it was appropriate for the MUHC
to wait for the outcome of the Review committee’s work, before letting
Plaintiff return to the RVH. The reality is that Plaintiff’s conduct was not
held to warrant disciplinary measures and that therefore, the Site Director or
the Head of Department cannot rightfully refuse to reintegrate him by
continuing to raise the October 2019 incident.

[
267
]

More generally, the Court finds MUHC’s inaction in this file
regrettable. Albeit with a clearly incomplete understanding of the role which
was played by all intervenors in the file, it is inescapable that the MUHC has
let this matter fester and continues to do so.

[
268
]

Indeed, despite the clear recommendations and prescient report in
2014, there are still today no formal department rules to which all are bound.
These rules can be imposed by the MUHC. They appear not to have done so. As a
result, there are endless discussions on the proper rules for on-call duty, for
allocation of resources including respiratory technicians, on days off. In
response to an undertaking to provide by-laws, rules, policy, etc., regarding
respiratory therapists’ allocation, the MUHC confirmed: that “no such
documentation exists and that many aspects of the daily functions are based on
patient needs, collegiality and “oral traditions” which are themselves based on
successful adaptations and adjusted to new realities and constraints”.
[172]

[
269
]

The lack of rules creates numerous occasions for runs-ins and
misunderstandings. Such a
modus vivendi
, in a highly charged atmosphere,
is untenable. Sidorowicz announced in her examination that rules and
regulations will most likely be adopted shortly. The Court hopes for the sake
of all involved that this will indeed occur.

[
270
]

Also, the MUHC appears to have, in all impunity, allowed the Head of
Department to organize a boycott of Plaintiff in all anesthesia departments on
October 17, 2020, at the same time as a Medical Examiner is mandated to carry
out an investigation into the Site Director’s complaint.

[
271
]

In its evidence, the MUHC also attempted to depict the Plaintiff as
making wild and unsubstantiated accusations regarding Daloze’s behaviour
towards residents and respiratory technicians.

[
272
]

As already discussed in detail, the information which was submitted
to the Court was clearly selective and did not allow the Court to have a full
picture. Thanks, in part, to Buu’s Frank testimony, this story was put into its
proper light.

[
273
]

The Court finds it extremely unfortunate that the complaints of
female residents regarding inappropriate behaviour are dealt with in the manner
set out in the proceedings. The Court is left with the distinct impression that
very serious concerns by learners, who are placed in a highly delicate position
with regard to the Site Director, are used as instruments for the purposes of
litigation. This is not fair to the learners and it is not fair to the Site
Director.

[
274
]

Given such events, it is incomprehensible that the MUHC would
present Plaintiff’s comments at the October 17 meeting to be without substance
and for Schricker to suggest that Plaintiff is delusional.

[
275
]

Hence, on this basis, the Court would have no doubt whatsoever to
come to the conclusion that not only does Plaintiff have an apparent right, but
that he has a clear right to be reinstated fully in his position.

1.3.2

Right to be entitled to the accommodations sought by Plaintiff’
specialist

[
276
]

It is however at this juncture that matters are complicated by
Plaintiff’s position.

[
277
]

Plaintiff does not want to be fully reinstituted as a full active
member. He wants to be reintegrated progressively, with significant
accommodations. He wants to decide when and how he will return as a fully
active member.

[
278
]

On the basis of the facts, the Court does not believe that a duty to
accommodate would extend as far.

[
279
]

Plaintiff on the one hand claims that his condition does not prevent
him from carrying out his duties at the RVH. Indeed, he has been exercising his
profession at the Private Clinic for over nine months at a rhythm of four days
a week.

[
280
]

Nevertheless, his physician indicates that the accommodations which
he imposes are not sought because of Plaintiff’s medical condition, but because
of the tension in the department which could have deleterious effects on his
condition. His ability to deal with the tension will dictate in large part at
what pace he will move to the full exercise of his privileges.

[
281
]

Paraphrasing Justice Deschamps in
Hydro Québec
, the MUHC must
not change privileges in a fundamental way. Plaintiff must be able to carry out
his clinical load, with the resources at hand and do on-call duty.

[
282
]

In a university health centre setting, the Court believes that
removing call duties, and working three set days a week goes beyond simple
accommodations of an active member’s workplace or duties. It in fact
constitutes a fundamental rearrangement of privileges. If Plaintiff does not
have to do call duty and can dictate his work schedule, others will have to
make up for it.

[
283
]

On the other hand, if Plaintiff is not given at least an opportunity
to return part time to the RVH, he will not be able to determine that he is
fit.

[
284
]

The Court believes that Plaintiff meets the “critère généralement
peu exigeant” to establish a serious issue to be tried, namely, that the
obligation to accommodate encompasses an obligation to attempt a progressive
reintegration.

[
285
]

In 2019, increasing pressure was brought to bear on Plaintiff for
him to resume his full duties as active member. The MUHC had shown patience and
understanding over close to two years after Plaintiff’s 2017 leave of absence.
It was becoming more insistent.

[
286
]

Plaintiff, on recommendation of his physician, now wants to turn the
clocks back to zero and begin anew a slow ramping up. Taking on call duty is
again a very distant objective.

[
287
]

As Justice Abella indicates in
Caron
, the undue hardship
threshold means an employer will always bear some sort of hardship.

[
288
]

The Court believes that offering some degree of progressive
reintegration maintains the symmetry between accommodation on the one hand and
undue hardship on the other.

[
289
]

This process of reintegration has to be limited in scope and in
time. Such a limited period may cause hardship, but not undue hardship.

[
290
]

The open ended conditions his specialist wants to impose, although
medically prudent, will very possibly constitute undue hardship and these
considerations must be weighed in the analysis of the balance of
inconveniences.

[
291
]

Before carrying out this balancing exercise, the Court must first
determine whether Plaintiff is suffering irreparable harm.

2.

Irreparable
harm

[
292
]

The Court believes that Plaintiff has shown that the situation is
indeed causing him an irreparable harm.

[
293
]

Plaintiff is not practicing at a tertiary or quaternary hospital
since over one year. The MUHC itself in its mission statement explains in how
the work it does is unique. As this mission statement highlights, the work
carried out in a private clinic such as the one where Plaintiff is relegated
since ten months is in no way comparable insofar as the complexity of the
clinical cases are concerned.

[
294
]

Plaintiff cannot teach. He cannot do research.

[
295
]

The honourable Blanchard found in
Azar
, the fact that
Plaintiff Azar lost a significant part of privileges has “comme conséquence
qu'Azar pratique presque de façon solitaire au sein du CHUM et qu'il a
maintenant une pratique très limitée.” This was found
to cause an irreparable harm.
[173]

In the present case, Plaintiff is in no different position when he is relegated
to the Private Clinic.

[
296
]

The MUHC claims that there is no irreparable harm and cites in
support of its position the TAQ’s decision in
N.R.
[174]

In that matter, the
hospital centre had revoked a cardiologist’s privileges and, as contemplated by
the
AHSS
, the cardiologist was contesting her revocation before the TAQ.
She was seeking a stay of the revocation, alleging
inter
alia
that: “l’impossibilité de maintenir ses compétences au niveau actuel
en raison d’une sous-utilisation de ses acquis, la perte du contact avec les confrères
d’autres spécialités (…) et la perte de son poste d’enseignante”.
[175]
It
was held by the administrative judge that this could not constitute irreparable
harm.

[
297
]

In contrast, in
Portnoy
, the Superior Court held that
preventing university teaching, research and the impact on reputation does
constitute irreparable harm.
[176]

[
298
]

The Court is therefore convinced that Plaintiff suffers irreparable
harm as a result of not being able to exercise its privileges at the RVH, or
any of the MUHC sites.

3.

Balance
of convenience

[
299
]

The inconveniences which are caused to Plaintiff flow directly from
the elements raised in the analysis of the irreparable harm. Plaintiff is being
prevented from carrying out his privileges at a university health center which
carries out tertiary and quaternary care. He cannot exercise his sub-speciality
in TEE. He cannot teach. He cannot carry out his research.

[
300
]

The Court finds that these are very substantial inconveniences.

[
301
]

The MUHC replies that it would suffer generate prejudices if it were
to progressively reintegrate Plaintiff. It raises issues of patient safety, the
hardship caused by Plaintiff’s refusal to carry out call and to dictate his
schedule, the threat to harmonious relations within his department, and the
risk to residents.

[
302
]

Patient safety must be paramount. The Court sees no risk whatsoever
to patients. The MUHC has made no evidence that patients are at risk. Such an
argument would indeed be very odd in a context where the MUHC relegates
Plaintiff to a Private Clinic where it contends complex anesthesia work is
carried out, without any supervision or administration.

[
303
]

The threat to harmonious relationships have indeed been considered
by Courts when weighing inconveniences.
[177]

However, the only evidence that is provided in this regard is that the Site
Director does not want Plaintiff back under any circumstances and that he
states that he will resign if Plaintiff does return. The Head of Department,
who wants Plaintiff removed since several years, also does not want him back
either.

[
304
]

As the Court has already explained, substantially modifying
Plaintiff’s privileges can only be done through the disciplinary mechanisms of
the
AHSS
. It would be inconsistent, in analysing inconveniences, to
consider what the law does not authorize. This is precisely why, when there is
a clear right, the Court of Appeal has stated in
HRM Projet Children inc
.
that this clear right “peut faire pencher la préponderance des inconvénients
dans le cadre de la pondération requise selon ce critère”.
[178]
If the MUHC considers that
Plaintiff conducts himself in such a manner that his return is impossible, then
it must consider disciplinary measures. This is not an inconvenience; it is
what the
AHSS
dictates.

[
305
]

In any event, the Court is not satisfied that it is Plaintiff who is
responsible for the difficult relations in the Department. It is Schricker who
appears since many years to want to get rid of the “group of five”.
Furthermore, the Review Committee notes that Plaintiff “has expressed regret
for the conversation he had with you and we trust the situation will not be
repeated”. It appears to be the Site Director who is intransigent and will not
consider any return of Plaintiff in the RVH department. However, his complaint
was dismissed.

[
306
]

Finally, a member of the group of five has signed an affidavit
whereby he states unequivocally: “I have not noticed any change in the
atmosphere of the Department of Anesthesia of the RVH since Dr. Water’s leave
of absence”.
[179]

[
307
]

Taking into consideration all these facts, the Court finds that
reinstating progressively Plaintiff would not disrupt a supposed “harmony”
within the RVH Department of Anesthesia.

[
308
]

The Court also finds the evidence highly unsatisfactory as to the
alleged inconveniences to residents. Residents should clearly not be drawn into
the conflict between pooled (the AA partners) and unpooled (group of five)
physicians. It is clearly disheartening for them to be privy to cynical remarks
about the profession. Plaintiff should abstain from either behaviour.

[
309
]

However, clearly, the LE Report evidences that the problems the
residents raise are far broader than these two improper comments by Plaintiff.
The fact that a large part of the LE Report is blacked out attests to this.

[
310
]

The Court is also surprised at how quickly the Faculty of Medicine
comes to the conclusion that the widespread discontent is now resolved. The
Court hopes, for all involved, and in particular for the residents, that this
is the case. None of the evidence however rationally permits the Court to
conclude that it is Plaintiff’s presence, as opposed to all others associate
professors, which would cause inconveniences to the residents.

[
311
]

Ultimately, the element which is must truly preoccupy the Court in
weighing inconveniences is the impact the order may have on the other
physicians regarding call, respiratory technicians and fixed days off.

[
312
]

Call is a key issue and has far reaching effects. Physicians spend
nights and week-ends carrying it out. The Court has no doubt this is taxing.
The Court does not accept Plaintiff’s argument that given that there are twenty
other physicians, for him not to assume call duties does not cause significant
inconveniences. The
AHSS
sets out that call roster is a fundamental part
of organizing medical resources.

[
313
]

On the other hand, it must be recognized that, presently, Plaintiff
is not carrying out call. Hence, whether he is at the RVH or at the Private
Clinic, this changes nothing from a practical standpoint for the other
physicians.

[
314
]

If in the long run he cannot carry out call, this will have to be
addressed either through administrative sanctions set out in duly approved
rules and regulations, disciplinary sanctions or at renewal of his privileges.
Call is not, in the very particular circumstances of this case, a consideration
in weighing inconveniences.

[
315
]

Insofar as respiratory technicians are concerned, the Court notes
the following response in the examination of Sidorowicz:
[180]

A- Well, I probably gave him the content verbally of Dr. Ginsberg's
letter. But, again, you know, as Dr. Daloze has probably explained to you, in
Quebec there's supposed to be an RT in the OR with the - with the physician,
with the anaesthetist, correct? So, here there was a request to ensure that
should an RT not be in the room for whatever reason, that somebody would be
available, you know. So, that's...

Q- So, that is a requirement in Quebec, it's standard practice to
have an RT in the room...

A- Yes.

Q- ... with the anaesthetist, yes?

A- Yes, exactly, yes.

Q- Okay. So, this isn't really an addition, this is just something
that you would expect to have in any case?

A- Yes.

[
316
]

What Plaintiff is asking is not to have a respiratory technician
present at all times, but rather “that the head respiratory technician contact
Plaintiff to check with her if any form of back-up is necessary”. Given
Sidorowicz’s testimony, this cannot be seen as an inconvenience.

[
317
]

Finally, as regards Plaintiff’s schedule, the Court notes that set
days are very difficult to reconcile with a tertiary or quaternary university
health centre.

[
318
]

The Court notes that taking predetermined
personal days is a serious issue at the RVH Anesthesia Department. In October
2019, Schricker writes to the physician staff the following:

you know the MUHC, like other Institutions providing quaternary care in this

members of the Department take personal days.

[
319
]

By imposing fixed working days schedule, the Court understands that
very significant inconveniences will be caused to the Department and all
physicians involved.

[
320
]

The proposal of working the first four weeks on Thursdays, then in
the following four weeks on Wednesdays and Thursdays and finally in the next
four weeks on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays will put considerable strain on
the department.

[
321
]

The inconveniences caused to the MUHC are certainly not negligible,
but no evidence has been provided that they will not be manageable, if they are
for a limited time. They will possibly constitute hardship, but not undue
hardship.

[
322
]

The Court understands that the Department of Anesthesia works on a
calendar month basis, and therefore, the Court will order that Plaintiff be
reintegrated at the RVH site progressively on Thursdays in June, Wednesdays and
Thursdays in July and Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays in August. The other
days, Plaintiff will work at the Private Clinic.

[
323
]

The Court cannot accept, however, what Plaintiff then proposes after
his three month period. His return cannot be open ended. This is simply
unrealistic.

[
324
]

The Court considers that Plaintiff must then be ready to decide,
with his physician, if he is ready to take a four day case load on the days the
MUHC requires him to be present. In November 2021, he must be ready to commit
to a five day load.

[
325
]

If he is not willing or able to so commit, the Court is of the
opinion that the balance of inconveniences would then lean in favour of the
MUHC, and the present order will cease to be in effect.

[
326
]

With regard to respiratory technicians, given the testimony of
Sidorowicz, the Court will order the MUHC to provide the accommodation sought,
as this is not really an accommodation.

[
327
]

As regards the assignments to cardiac surgery, starting June,
Plaintiff will assume a half load every two weeks as sought in the
accommodations. As of November, for this order to continue to be in effect, he
must return be a full load unless the MUHC agrees to a lesser load.

[
328
]

As of November, Plaintiff will also have to be ready to take a full
on-call duty, on the condition that the MUHC has adopted department rules and
regulations. If these rules are not adopted, Plaintiff cannot be called as to
carry out call.

4.

Final
remarks

[
329
]

It is therefore in carrying out this very delicate balancing act
that the Court renders its conclusions.

[
330
]

The present judgment will apply until the earlier of final judgment
or the expiry of Plaintiff’s present privileges, as extended by the effect of
the “état d’urgence sanitaire”.

[
331
]

Finally, the Court will not render any conclusions regarding
defamation. The Court does not believe it is proper for the MUHC to be held,
with a possible sanction of contempt, to control what the Head of Department or
the Site Director say. Also, the open ended conclusion to “stop its
administration… from damaging Dr. Water’s reputation” is not appropriate and
will trigger litigation rather than providing clear direction.
